transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: Potter. You were ordered to wait for backup. Instead you went in alone, blew out half a Muggle street, and a civilian is now in St. Mungo's with magical burns. Being the Boy Who Lived doesn't exempt you from protocol. What were you thinking?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I... I'm sorry, sir. I know I should have followed orders. It was just that... the Death Eater was about to get away. I couldn't let that happen. But I understand now that I put others at risk. It was a mistake, and I take full responsibility.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: "Sorry" doesn't quite cut it, Potter. Not when we've got a magically burnt Muggle in St. Mungo's and half a street looking like a dragon sneezed on it. You couldn't let him get away, you say? And what about the civilian now paying the price for your impatience? The whole point of the protocol, the *backup*, is to minimise collateral damage, to ensure the safety of *everyone*, not just to bag a suspect. Your 'full responsibility' doesn't unburn that woman, does it? So I ask again, what *exactly* was going through your head when you decided to ignore a direct order and go in like a bull in a china shop?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Sir, I... I know what I did was wrong. I was thinking about the mission, about stopping the Death Eater, and I didn't consider the possible consequences. I should have. I should have waited for backup like I was ordered to. I'm... I'm sorry for the civilian, for the damage. It wasn't supposed to happen this way. I'll do whatever it takes to make it right.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
"Not supposed to happen this way" is a luxury we don't have in this job, Potter. You don't get to hand-wave away the fallout because your intentions were pure. Good intentions pave the road to St. Mungo's, as we're seeing. The mission isn't just about the target; it's about the execution, the containment, the *aftermath*. You didn't just 'not consider' the consequences; you actively disregarded the very system put in place to *prevent* them.

"Whatever it takes to make it right," you say? And what exactly would that be? You want to visit Mrs. Higgins in St. Mungo's and explain why she's got a nice magical burn courtesy of the Auror Department? Or perhaps you'd like to help the Ministry explain to the Muggles why their homes spontaneously combusted? This isn't a classroom where a sincere apology wipes the slate clean. This is real, and the stakes are real. So let's talk about the *real* thought process. Why, despite knowing the rules, despite understanding the risks, did you still believe *you* were the exception to the rule? What made you think you knew better than the direct order you were given?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You're right, sir. I was... I was acting on instinct. I've always felt the need to act, to do something when I see a threat. It's like... when I was a kid, I was always running into situations I shouldn't have been in. I've spent so much of my life *reacting* to what's happening around me that I guess I'm not used to waiting, to following orders. I know that's no excuse. It's not a reason to put others at risk. I'm... I'm working on it. I want to be a better Auror, to follow the rules, to not let my... my need to act overrule my judgment. I'm sorry for the damage, for the risk I took. I'm ready to face the consequences.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
"Acting on instinct." "Always felt the need to act." "Not used to waiting." Potter, you're an Auror, not a bloody untrained wizard on the run anymore. Your 'instincts' are precisely what we train out of you in this department. We teach you discipline, procedure, the importance of coordinated action, not some heroic, lone-wolf charge that leaves civilians paying the price.

You've spent your life reacting? Fine. But you're in a professional department now, with professional responsibilities. That "kid who ran into situations" needs to grow up, and grow up fast, if he expects to remain an Auror. Your past trauma, your personal history – none of that exempts you from the basic duty of protecting the public, which you very clearly failed to do in this instance.

"Working on it" isn't going to cut it when lives are on the line, Potter. This isn't a therapy session. This is a disciplinary matter. You say you want to be a better Auror. Prove it. Because right now, what I'm seeing is a liability who can't follow a simple order and is causing more problems than he solves. Your 'need to act' nearly got a Muggle killed. That's not a trait we value here. What steps are you *actually* taking to curb this impulse? Because if it happens again, your career as an Auror will be over. Understood?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Yes, sir, I understand. I'm... I'm taking this very seriously. I know that what I did was wrong, and I'm not trying to make excuses. I want to be the best Auror I can be. I'm seeing a therapist to work on my... my issues with acting impulsively. I'm also working with my team to develop better communication and decision-making strategies. I'm trying to internalize the protocols so that they become second nature, not something I override in a moment of... of... I don't know, bravery? stupidity? It's a work in progress, but I'm committed to it. I want to be an asset to the department, not a liability. I want to be someone who can be counted on to do the right thing, not just the thing that seems right in the moment.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
Therapy and team strategies are a start, Potter, but I need to see results, not just intentions. "Work in progress" doesn't cover the medical bills, does it? "Bravery or stupidity" is a distinction you need to make *before* you blow up a street, not in my office afterwards. We need Aurors who make the right call *in the moment*, not just in hindsight.

Internalising protocols isn't a suggestion; it's a requirement for anyone wearing this badge. If they're not second nature, then you're not ready for the field. Not for missions that involve Muggles, civilians, or anything less than a deserted island.

You say you want to be an asset. You say you want to be counted on. This incident, however, points to the exact opposite. It shows a disregard for orders, a failure in judgment, and a significant risk to the public we are sworn to protect. For now, you're off active duty, effective immediately. You'll be assigned to desk work, reviewing past cases, until I see tangible proof that you can follow procedure without endangering others. And I'll be speaking with your team leader about implementing stricter oversight on your future assignments, should you ever return to the field. Is that clear?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Yes, sir, it's clear. I... I accept the decision. I'll do the best I can with the desk work, and I'll prove that I can follow the rules, that I can be a responsible Auror. I'm... I'm grateful for the second chance, even if it's just to sit at a desk. I'll make the most of it, and I'll be ready when you decide I can go back out into the field. I'll show you that I can do this, that I can be the Auror you want me to be.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
It's not a "second chance" in the way you might think, Potter. It's a reprieve, a last opportunity to demonstrate you understand the gravity of this job and your place within it. Your gratitude is noted, but frankly, I'm more interested in seeing a change in behaviour.

Desk work is not a punishment to be 'made the most of'; it's an opportunity for you to re-engage with the foundational principles of Auror work, to understand the meticulous planning and careful execution that precedes *every* field operation. Use this time to internalise those protocols, not just intellectually, but instinctually. You need to understand *why* we have them, and why disregarding them has such severe consequences.

"The Auror I want you to be" is an Auror who follows orders, protects civilians, and understands that the greater good often means exercising restraint, not just charging in. Your actions will speak louder than any apologies or promises you make in this office. Now, report to Auror Davies for your new assignments. And don't make me regret this, Potter. Dismissed.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Understood, sir. I'll report to Auror Davies right away. I... I appreciate the opportunity to demonstrate my understanding of the protocols. I won't let you down. I'll show you that I can be an Auror who makes the right calls, who follows the rules, who prioritizes the safety of civilians above all else. Thank you for this... this chance to prove myself. I'll be ready when you decide to send me back out.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
I expect nothing less, Potter. Your appreciation is irrelevant compared to the concrete demonstration of competence and discipline that I expect to see. This isn't about 'proving yourself' to me; it's about proving yourself capable of holding the responsibilities of an Auror.

You'll be ready when I decide you're ready, and that decision will be based solely on your performance and your adherence to procedure during this period. Go.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Sir, I... I'll do everything I can to meet those expectations. I'll be meticulous in my work, thorough in my reviews, and I'll show you that I can be counted on to do the job right. I'll earn my way back into the field, not just for myself, but for the department, for the public we're supposed to protect. I'll see you when I'm ready, sir. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: Right. You will. And I expect nothing less. Your work will be scrutinised, Potter. Every report, every review. Don't think for a moment this is a holiday. Earn your way back, not with promises, but with demonstrable, consistent adherence to the standards of this department. Now, get to Auror Davies. That's an order.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Yes, sir. I understand. I'll get to work right away. I'll show you that I can meet those standards, that I can be the Auror you and the department need me to be. I'll... I'll prove that I can do this job safely, effectively, and with the respect for protocol it requires. Thank you, sir. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: Potter. You've said your piece. Now go. Your actions from this point forward will speak for themselves. This conversation is over.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Understood, sir. I'm... I'm ready to get to work. I'll... I'll do my best to show you that I can be an asset to the department. I'll report to Auror Davies immediately. Thank you for... for not giving up on me completely. Goodbye, sir.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: Potter, I gave you an order. Report to Auror Davies. Immediately. Now.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Yes, sir. I'm on my way to see Auror Davies. I'm... I'm committed to showing you that I can be a reliable, disciplined member of the team. I'll do the work, and I'll do it well. Goodbye, sir.

Openness.behavioral_evidence: Harry admits to an instinctual, reactive approach: 'I've spent so much of my life *reacting*... I'm not used to waiting, to following orders.' He is also willing to explore new strategies for improvement ('seeing a therapist to work on my... issues with acting impulsively').

Conscientiousness.behavioral_evidence: He explicitly states, 'I didn't consider the possible consequences. I should have.' This demonstrates a failure in planning, foresight, and adherence to protocol, leading to significant collateral damage.

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Harry is highly action-oriented, stating, 'I've always felt the need to act, to do something when I see a threat.' He remains verbally engaged and assertive throughout the confrontational discussion.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: He repeatedly apologizes ('I'm sorry, sir'), takes full responsibility, says 'You're right, sir,' and expresses gratitude for the chance to improve, demonstrating a strong desire to please and cooperate.

Neuroticism.behavioral_evidence: Harry reveals he is 'seeing a therapist to work on my... my issues with acting impulsively,' indicating an ongoing struggle with emotional regulation and impulse control. His frequent hesitations ('I... I'm sorry') also suggest internal discomfort.
